Polycystic ovary syndrome (PCOS)

Two rat studies report more follicles and corpora lutea and fewer ovarian cysts or altered hormone measures. Two donated-oocyte experiments report changes in maturation and laboratory markers. Clinical benefit for women has not been tested.

Certainty of evidence (estimate)

Low certainty for PCOS-related ovarian changes in rat models (Alves et al. 2019; Polat et al. 2023).

Very low certainty for menstrual, metabolic, or fertility benefits in women; the available human-derived evidence comes from laboratory oocyte experiments, not clinical treatment studies (Sahraeian et al. 2023; Sahraeian et al. 2024).

Summary of the Evidence

Four relevant publications were identified: two rat experiments and two laboratory studies using donated oocytes from women with PCOS. The two oocyte experiments come from the same research group. No clinical trial has tested PBM as treatment for women with PCOS.

Human and clinical evidence

No study was identified in which women with PCOS received PBM as treatment. The two laboratory publications used donated oocytes from women with PCOS, but the treatment took place outside the body and did not assess menstrual regularity, ovulation, insulin resistance, androgen symptoms, pregnancy, or live birth.

Animal evidence

In an estradiol-valerate rat model, PBM increased plasma progesterone and testosterone, lowered luteinizing hormone, increased ovarian follicles and corpora lutea, and reduced ovarian cysts. A separate rat dose-response study reported that 2 J/cm² produced the most favorable combination of measured ovarian and hormonal outcomes, while its dose and exposure-time reporting was not fully consistent (Alves et al. 2019; Polat et al. 2023).

In-vitro and ex-vivo evidence

The two same-group studies of donated PCOS oocytes reported higher maturation or fertilization measures and changes in glutathione, oxidative stress, apoptosis/autophagy markers, acetylation, or miRNA expression. One protocol also used extracellular vesicles, so its outcomes cannot be attributed to PBM alone. (Sahraeian et al. 2023; Sahraeian et al. 2024).

Treatment Parameters and Generalizability

The rat studies used repeated local exposure, including 904-nm near-infrared light at 1, 2, or 6 J/cm² and a separate protocol with different local ovarian delivery. The donated-oocyte experiment used 640-nm red visible light at 1.85 J/cm². The models and doses are not directly comparable, and no head-to-head study has identified a transferable treatment schedule for patients.

Interpretation

The animal and laboratory studies report changes in different reproductive measures. They do not show whether PBM improves symptoms, fertility, or metabolic outcomes in women with PCOS.

Rationale for the certainty assessment

Two rat experiments report changes in ovarian and hormonal measures (Alves et al. 2019; Polat et al. 2023). Two laboratory studies of donated PCOS oocytes report changes in selected maturation and biochemical outcomes (Sahraeian et al. 2023; Sahraeian et al. 2024). These animal and laboratory outcomes do not establish clinical benefit. Studies in women measuring menstrual cycles, ovulation, metabolic outcomes, and pregnancy would clarify clinical relevance.
